quests.instruction: Which link may get an extra /r/ in some accents, even though no r is written?
quests.textToSpeak: it was my idea of fun
quests.hint: A word ending in a weak vowel meets a vowel. Which pair?
quests.explanation: In some non-rhotic accents speakers put a small /r/ between 'idea' and 'of', saying 'idear of', even though no r is written. In rhotic accents that is not heard. It is worth recognising but not something you need to produce.
quests.flowRule: Intrusive /r/ (accent-dependent): In some non-rhotic accents speakers add an /r/ between a word ending in /ə/, /ɑː/ or /ɔː/ and a following vowel even when no r is written (idea of sounds like 'idear of'). It is common in those accents and absent in others, so it is useful to recognise but not something you need to produce.

quests.textToSpeak: I saw it on the news
quests.hint: A word ending in a long open vowel meets another vowel.

quests.instruction: Which link carries a linking /r/?
quests.hint: Two words in the sentence could invite an /r/. Only one has an r in the spelling.
quests.explanation: 'Her' ends in a written r, so the /r/ is genuinely there before 'over' in most accents. 'Saw her' offers no vowel at all, because 'her' begins with /h/. A written r is the clue that separates a linking /r/ from an intrusive one.
quests.flowRule: Linking /r/ (accent-dependent): In rhotic accents (most of North America, Scotland, Ireland) a word-final r is always pronounced, so it simply connects to a following vowel. In non-rhotic accents (for example most of England, Australia, New Zealand) the r is silent before a consonant or a pause but usually returns before a vowel, as in 'far away'. Either way, the two words connect.

quests.instruction: Which word-final r connects to the next vowel?
quests.textToSpeak: the drawer and the sofa arrived today
quests.hint: Which boundary could carry an /r/ across, because of the spelling?
quests.explanation: 'Drawer' ends in a written r, so 'drawer and' has a linking /r/ in most accents. 'Sofa arrived' has no r in its spelling, so any /r/ there would be intrusive. The spelling is the guide.

quests.instruction: Which link is a glide between two vowels, not a consonant link?
quests.hint: Skip the consonant links. Where does one vowel run straight into another?
quests.explanation: 'Try' ends in /aɪ/ and 'it' begins with /ɪ/, so a light /j/ glides across; no consonant is released. 'It on' is the consonant link in this sentence, carried by /t/.
quests.flowRule: Vowel-to-Vowel Linking with a /j/ glide: After vowels made with the tongue high and forward (/iː/, /eɪ/, /aɪ/, /ɔɪ/), many speakers slide through a light /j/ ('y') before the next vowel. It is a natural transition, not a written letter, and it is subtle.

quests.instruction: Find the connection between two vowel sounds
quests.hint: A question about identity. Which pair has a vowel on both sides?
quests.explanation: 'Who' ends in /uː/ and 'are' begins with a vowel, so a faint /w/ eases between them. 'Are you' does not link, because /r/ meets /j/. The glide is the point of the question.
quests.flowRule: Vowel-to-Vowel Linking with a /w/ glide: After vowels made with rounded lips (/uː/, /əʊ/, /aʊ/), many speakers slide through a light /w/ before the next vowel. It is a natural transition, not a written letter, and it is subtle.

quests.hint: Which link has no consonant between its two sounds?

quests.instruction: Where do two sounds blend into one in fast, informal speech?
quests.hint: Which pair merges into a new sound?
quests.explanation: 'Got you' sounds like 'gotcha' as /t/ and /j/ merge into /tʃ/. 'Covered' has no link. In this question, the sound at the boundary itself changes.
quests.flowRule: Yod-coalescence (informal speech): When a word ending in /t/, /d/, /s/ or /z/ is followed by 'you' or 'your', the two sounds often merge into one: /t/+/j/ becomes /tʃ/ ('got you' sounds like 'gotcha'), /d/+/j/ becomes /dʒ/ ('did you' like 'didja'), /s/+/j/ becomes /ʃ/ and /z/+/j/ becomes /ʒ/. This is a normal informal reduction, not a mistake, and careful speakers may keep the sounds apart.

quests.instruction: Where does a final /t/, /d/ or /n/ shift to match the next sound?
quests.hint: Which pair's first word changes its last sound?
quests.explanation: Before /m/ the /n/ of 'one' often moves towards /m/, giving 'wum more'. 'Just one' does not link, because 'one' begins with /w/. A small change like this passes unnoticed in fast speech.
quests.flowRule: Place assimilation (informal speech): At the end of a word, /t/, /d/ and /n/ often take on the place of the next sound. Before /p b m/ they shift towards lip sounds (ten people sounds like 'tem people'; bad back like 'bab back'), and before /k g/ towards back-of-the-mouth sounds (in case like 'ing case'). It is common in fast speech and listeners barely notice it.

quests.instruction: Where does a /t/ or /d/ drop out between two consonants?
quests.hint: Which pair loses a consonant in fast speech?
quests.explanation: The /t/ of 'last' is often dropped before /n/, so you hear 'las night'. 'Got home' does not link at all, because /t/ meets /h/.
quests.flowRule: Elision (informal speech): A /t/ or /d/ between two other consonants is often left out in fast speech, so 'next day' sounds like 'nex day' and 'old man' like 'ol man'. The words still connect smoothly; the consonant cluster simply gets lighter.

quests.instruction: Which pair seems to join two vowels in spelling but does not in sound?
quests.textToSpeak: she works for a university abroad
quests.hint: Think about which article you would use before the second word. That tells you how it begins.
quests.explanation: 'University' begins with /j/, which is why we say 'a', not 'an', and why nothing joins. 'For a' and 'university abroad' are the real links in this sentence.
quests.flowRule: Sound, not spelling (glides): Spelling can suggest a vowel-to-vowel link where there is none. 'One' begins with /w/ and 'unique' with /j/, so they are consonant sounds. Check the first sound of a word, not its first letter.

quests.instruction: Which pair would sound broken with a pause between the words?
quests.textToSpeak: could you hold the door open
quests.hint: A request at a door. One pair has an r-sound before a vowel.
quests.explanation: 'Door' ends in an /r/ for rhotic speakers, and non-rhotic speakers add it before the vowel of 'open'. Either way the pair runs together, and a pause would make a polite request sound stiff.
quests.flowRule: Smooth versus separated speech: Fluent speakers keep a phrase in one flow and pause only between thought groups. A gap inside a linked pair sounds choppy even when every word is clear, so train your ear to hear the join rather than the separate words.
